title: What Happens When You Click a Link
description: Trace the step-by-step lifecycle of navigating the web: DNS resolution, TCP handshake, HTTP request/response exchange, HTML parsing, subresource discovery, and DOM tree construction.

objectives.statement: Sequence the technical milestones from clicking a link to rendering a webpage in the browser.
Explain how the browser discovers and requests secondary resources (CSS, JS, images) during HTML parsing.

content.title: Under the Hood of a Single Click
content.hook: You click a link and in half a second a new world appears. But beneath that single tap lies a complex technical sequence across computers worldwide.
content.context: Before the browser can render even one pixel of text, it must convert domain names to IP addresses (DNS), establish secure encrypted connections (TCP/TLS), fetch the root HTML document, parse its tags into a DOM tree, and initiate subresource requests for stylesheets, scripts, and fonts.
goals: Understand how DNS converts human-friendly URLs into machine IP addresses.
Sequence the stages of network transport and HTML document parsing.
Identify how secondary asset requests (CSS, JS, images) are triggered.

content.title: The Navigation Pipeline
content.description: Step 1: DNS Lookup (forge.dev -> 192.0.2.1). Step 2: TCP/TLS Handshake. Step 3: HTTP GET Request. Step 4: Server Response (HTML payload). Step 5: Parser discovers <link rel="stylesheet"> and <script> -> triggers subresource network requests.

content.prompt: Arrange the following milestones in chronological order from the moment a user clicks a link until the browser parses the HTML:

items.text: DNS Lookup (Resolving domain name to server IP address)
TCP/TLS Handshake (Establishing secure connection to server)
HTTP GET Request sent over the connection
Server returns HTTP 200 response with HTML payload
Browser parses HTML bytes and encounters subresource tags

feedback.correct: Outstanding! First DNS finds the IP, then TCP/TLS connects, then the HTTP GET is dispatched, then HTML arrives, and finally parsing discovers stylesheets and scripts.
feedback.incorrect: Review the networking pipeline: the browser cannot send an HTTP request before resolving the IP address (DNS) and establishing the connection (TCP/TLS).

options: The browser stops running and displays an error saying CSS is not allowed in HTML.
The browser pauses and cancels the HTML document download permanently.
The browser initiates a secondary asynchronous HTTP GET request for `/styles/main.css` across the network.
The browser executes the CSS code on the backend server before receiving it.

content.prompt: Why is it important for frontend developers to minimize the number and size of external stylesheets, scripts, and large images linked inside an HTML document?

feedback.correct: Spot on! Each linked asset requires network roundtrips, bandwidth, and parsing time. Heavy or blocking subresources delay the page's render time and degrade user experience.
feedback.incorrect: Consider the impact of multiple network requests and large payloads on page loading speed and responsiveness.
